abstract: |
  Can a graph neural network provide useful starting information for mixed-integer optimization? We investigate this question for capacitated facility location by learning binary solution values from variable-constraint graphs. Our class-aware procedure first selects variables predicted to take value 1, which are rare in this problem family, and then adds confident predictions of value 0. These values form a partial starting solution: Gurobi determines the remaining values and continues optimizing the unchanged model. The predictor is trained for 100 epochs on a quality-screened cohort of 54 original instances, using separate training, validation, and predictive-test partitions. It achieves pooled F1 of 0.6993 and average precision of 0.7745 on 5,536,400 binary targets. After qualifying the guidance policy on six medium validation instances, we evaluate it on six distinct medium test instances under a 3,600-second optimization budget. Comparisons include Gurobi without learned guidance and starting values selected from the root linear relaxation. Learned starts reduce the terminal relative MIP gap on five of six test instances, with a median improvement of 1.164 percentage points. Two learned-start runs finish before the time limit, while all unguided runs reach that limit. These findings demonstrate the practical potential of class-aware graph predictions in the examined setting and motivate broader evaluation across instances and computational budgets.
---

# Introduction

Capacitated facility location combines discrete facility decisions with allocation subject to capacity restrictions. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) provides a general framework for such decisions, but difficult instances may leave a substantial primal-dual gap after hours of computation. Repeated solution of a related problem family creates an opportunity to learn assignment patterns. The practical question is not merely whether those patterns are predictable: it is whether they improve a solver without compromising the mathematical problem or its certificates.

We examine this question using capacitated facility location (CFL) instances from MILPBench [@milpbench]. A graph neural network (GNN) learns to predict binary solution values from the relationships between variables and constraints. A subset of these predictions provides starting values to Gurobi. The remaining variables are left unspecified, allowing the solver to complete the candidate and continue its search. In this way, learning supplies information to the optimization process while the original constraints and variable domains remain intact.

The research question is: can starting values predicted by a bipartite GNN improve the solutions obtained within a fixed time budget on medium CFL instances not used to fit the network? We address it through a class-aware selection rule. Here, class-aware means that selection treats predicted values of 1 and 0 separately, so that the much more numerous zeros do not displace promising positive assignments. We compare this approach with Gurobi without supplied starting values and with starting values obtained from the root linear programming (LP) relaxation. The latter comparator specifies the same number of variables and the same number of ones as the learned start, making the source of the selected values the main distinction between them.

The study contributes a reproducible procedure connecting graph-based assignment prediction to native partial MIP starts, together with separate assessments of predictive performance and solver outcomes. @fig-pipeline summarizes this connection and distinguishes the offline learning stage from the online application to a new optimization instance.

![Offline learning and online solver guidance.](figures/figure_pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

Source: implemented learning and guidance procedure.

The upper row follows the preparation of checked solution labels, the construction of bipartite graphs, and network training. Validation then determines the checkpoint, decision threshold, and guidance policy. The lower row follows a new instance: a graph is constructed without its solution label, the frozen network predicts binary values, and selected values are submitted to a fresh Gurobi solve. The link between the rows represents the trained model and fixed selection policy, rather than access to the new instance's solution. Solver outcomes are evaluated only after this policy has been fixed.

# Related work

## Learning to Optimize

Learning to Optimize (L2O) uses experience from related problems to improve optimization algorithms. The methodological perspective of @bengio2021 distinguishes learning a useful solver decision from replacing the entire solution process. @chen2022primer discuss learned algorithms and their evaluation, while @chen2024tutorial organize applications around acceleration, solution estimation, and model adaptation. The present study belongs to solution-guided acceleration: the network proposes values and a mathematical solver checks and completes them.

Recent work illustrates several ways to supply learned information. @qu2026 develop an unsupervised approach for parameterized mixed-integer programs that uses learned patterns to derive additional constraints. @goerigk2025 predict relevant starting scenarios for robust combinatorial optimization. @tang2024l2o study solution generation for mixed-integer nonlinear problems with feasibility mechanisms. Our approach instead supplies selected binary values through the solver's native starting-solution interface, leaving the feasible region unchanged.

## Graph representations and solver decisions

The variable-constraint bipartite architecture of @gasse2019 provides our principal architectural foundation. It represents a mathematical program as interacting variable and constraint nodes. Whereas their network learns branching decisions, ours predicts binary values for a starting solution. @cappart2021 review the wider use of graph representations in combinatorial reasoning. Related applications include comparing search nodes [@labassi2022], predicting objective values [@scavuzzo2024], and selecting cutting planes with structured graph learning [@zhang2026]. These studies share an interest in exploiting problem structure, but the predicted object and its role in the solver differ.

Theoretical studies examine which optimization information graph architectures can represent. @chen2024branching analyze message-passing capacity for branching scores, and @chen2024quadratic study graph representations of quadratic programs. They motivate a task-specific design: the graph, learning target, and solver interface should be considered together.

## Primal guidance

Primal guidance seeks good feasible solutions during optimization. Examples include prediction-guided neighbourhood search [@ding2020], variable-bias guidance [@khalil2022], and GNN primal heuristics [@canturk2024]. Neural Diving also connects predicted partial assignments to an optimizer [@nair2020]. Local branching explores a neighbourhood around a feasible solution [@fischetti2003]. We use one checked solution per training instance as supervision and submit predictions through Gurobi's native `Start` attribute [@gurobi2026]. Unlike a restricted neighbourhood or fixed variable bounds, this interface offers a candidate to the solver without excluding other feasible solutions. Our focus is the selection of scarce positive predictions and its measured effect on fixed-budget CFL optimization.

# Proposed method

## Instances and labels

Let $p$ identify an original benchmark instance, referred to as a parent when tracking data lineage. Its mathematical program is

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_p^\star &= \min_x\; c_p^\top x+c_{p,0},\\
A_p x &\mathrel{\bowtie_p} b_p,\\
\ell_p\leq x &\leq u_p,\qquad x_j\in\mathbb Z\quad(j\in I_p).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $A_p$ and $b_p$ define the linear constraints, $c_p$ and $c_{p,0}$ the objective, and $I_p$ the integer variables. The symbol $\bowtie_p$ denotes each row's inequality or equality sense. The original identities, coefficients, bounds, row senses, and objective constant are preserved. All experiments explicitly set the objective sense to MINIMIZE, overriding the MAXIMIZE headers in the supplied files. Input hashes and both objective senses are recorded, so that this study's minimization convention can be reproduced. Variable predictions are aligned with the original column identities rather than an assumed naming convention.

Let $B_p\subseteq I_p$ contain the binary variables. A feasible incumbent, meaning the best feasible solution retained by the solver, supplies target values $y_{pj}\in\{0,1\}$. Before admitting a label, we check variable coverage, bounds, integrality, every linear constraint, and reconstruction of the objective value. We also require a finite terminal relative MIP gap no greater than 0.10. Thus, admitted labels are feasible solutions within the specified quality threshold; they may be approximate rather than optimal.

## Offline graph learning

Each variable and constraint becomes a node, connected whenever its coefficient in $A_p$ is nonzero. The edge carries that coefficient. Variable features describe the objective, bounds, type, and value in a Gurobi root-node LP relaxation captured through a MIPNODE callback. Constraint features describe the right-hand side and row sense. This representation brings together the local properties of each variable and its relationships with the constraints. Relaxation values are matched by variable identity, and feature construction uses no solution labels at prediction time.

The seven variable channels are transformed objective coefficient, lower bound, upper bound, three type indicators, and root value. The five row channels are transformed right-hand side, three sense indicators, and a constant. A single edge channel encodes the coefficient. Numerical coefficients and bounds use signed $\log(1+|t|)$ after clipping to $[-60000,60000]$; infinite bounds use the corresponding endpoint. Root values are clipped without logarithmic scaling. These numerical encodings affect learning inputs, not the original solver model; clipping counts are audited.

The Gasse-inspired network uses two message-passing layers with hidden dimension 32. Messages first update constraint representations and then return information to variable nodes. Input normalization is fitted on training graphs only, including variable-side normalization of the updated constraint messages. The final variable score $s_{pj}$ is transformed by the sigmoid function into $q_{pj}=\sigma(s_{pj})$. Training minimizes positive-class-weighted binary cross-entropy (BCE),

$$\ell_{pj}=-w_+y_{pj}\log\sigma(s_{pj})-(1-y_{pj})\log(1-\sigma(s_{pj})),$$

where $w_+$ is estimated from the training targets. BCE penalizes disagreement between predicted scores and binary labels; the extra weight increases the contribution of the rare positive class. Logarithmic scoring has a well-established basis in probabilistic prediction [@gneiting2007]. Class weighting is used here to learn useful assignments, and the resulting scores are assessed separately for calibration. Adam uses learning rate $10^{-3}$, gradient-norm clipping at 1, seed 42, and 100 epochs. Parent-balanced sampling draws each training parent four times per epoch. Validation weighted BCE selects the checkpoint, and validation F1 selects the threshold $\tau=0.9991843104362488$. The evaluation metrics are defined in @sec-metrics.

## Class-aware partial starts

For $q_j=\sigma(s_j)$, let $\hat y_j=\mathbf1[q_j\geq\tau]$. With $n=|B_p|$, define

$$K=\min\{n,20000,\max(1,\lfloor0.10n\rfloor)\}.$$

The support of a partial start is the set of variables for which values are supplied; $K$ is its maximum size. Selection first takes up to $K$ predicted ones in decreasing $q_j$ order, then fills any remaining places with predicted zeros in decreasing $1-q_j$ order. Variable names resolve ties consistently. This is the class-aware step: positive and negative predictions are ranked separately, giving priority to the scarce predicted ones. If no score reaches the positive threshold, the policy abstains. The 10% support fraction and 20,000-variable cap limit the amount of supplied information.

Selected values are assigned to Gurobi's `Start` attribute, while other values remain undefined. Gurobi then attempts to complete or repair this partial candidate as part of its solution process. We verify that the objective, matrix, row senses, and bounds have identical mathematical signatures before and after submission.

For comparison, the root-LP start uses the relaxation rather than the network to select variables. Suppose the GNN supplies $K'$ values, including $r$ ones. The comparator assigns 1 to the $r$ binary variables with the largest relaxation values and 0 to the $K'-r$ remaining variables with the smallest relaxation values. Both starts therefore supply equally many values with the same balance of ones and zeros. This matched construction helps examine whether learned variable selection adds useful information beyond that available from the LP relaxation.

# Experimental design

## Populations and information boundaries

The learning cohort contains 54 quality-screened original instances: 30 easy and 24 medium. It is divided into 34 training, ten validation, and ten predictive-test parents. @tbl-populations identifies the purpose of each partition and distinguishes predictive testing from the separate optimization comparison.

| Stage | Parents | Permitted information | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Fitting | 34 training originals | Admitted labels and graphs | Gradient updates and prenorm |
| Predictor selection | 10 validation originals | Labels and scores | Checkpoint and threshold |
| Predictive evaluation | 10 test originals: six easy, four medium | Held-out labels | Classification and ranking |
| Guidance qualification | Six medium validation originals | Label-free inference and optimization | Qualify fixed start policy |
| Optimization test | Six distinct medium test originals | Label-free inference and optimization | Frozen-policy comparison |

: Experimental populations and their roles. {#tbl-populations}

The table separates two questions: how accurately the network predicts values, and whether those predictions improve optimization. The same original instance retains its assigned role across every representation. Optimization-test parents are medium 0, 4, 7, 9, 12, and 20. Medium 9 and 20 do not have admitted predictive-test labels but retain their fixed test role. Their solver evaluation uses label-free graph construction, without adding them to network fitting or selection.

Guidance validation uses medium 5, 6, 11, 14, 17, and 19. Medium 5 and 6 similarly retain their validation role for label-free optimization despite lacking admitted graph-validation labels. The qualification rule is fixed before validation execution: six valid nonabstained starts, at least four terminal-gap improvements, a nonpositive median guided-minus-control difference, and at most one gap increase exceeding one percentage point. After qualification, the checkpoint, threshold, coverage, and ordering remain fixed for the optimization test.

## Comparisons and time measurements

Each parent is solved using three fresh Gurobi models: an unguided control, a matched root-LP start, and a class-aware GNN start. Parameters are identical apart from starting values: one solver thread, seed 42, a 3,600-second optimization limit, and relative stopping tolerance $10^{-4}$. Method order rotates across parents. Label-free root capture has a separate 600-second ceiling, and the returned incumbents undergo independent feasibility and objective checks.

The primary optimization outcome is the terminal relative MIP gap. It measures the distance between the best feasible objective $z^P$ and the solver's bound $z^D$ on the optimum. For finite nonzero $z^P$, we use $g=|z^P-z^D|/|z^P|$, with explicit handling of unavailable or degenerate values. A smaller gap indicates a tighter optimality certificate. For method $m$, the paired effect is $\Delta g_{pm}=g_{pm}-g_{p,\mathrm{control}}$; multiplying it by 100 gives a percentage-point difference. Negative differences favor guidance. Means, medians, win counts, and leave-out diagnostics summarize these paired observations.

Time measurements distinguish total worker elapsed time, source reading and verification, model construction, and optimization. LP parsing belongs to model construction; independent auditing and residual overhead are recorded separately. A cold application additionally includes feature preparation and network inference. A reusable-artifact application assumes these preparations have already been completed, while still verifying their artifacts. Offline training, scheduler waiting, and experiment orchestration are accounted for separately from online solver application.

We also record the first observed time at which gap becomes at most 10%. An observation is right-censored when the target has not been reached before monitoring ends: its attainment time is unknown beyond the available budget. Accordingly, a run ending at 3,600 seconds without crossing the target is not assigned an observed crossing time of 3,600 seconds. Time to optimality is treated separately; a run may cross 10% and still be censored for optimality. Callback timestamps identify the first observed crossing rather than an exact continuous-time event. The unit of the solver comparison is the original instance, whereas predictive metrics summarize its binary variables.

## Predictive evaluation metrics {#sec-metrics}

Predictive evaluation measures agreement with checked binary labels, ranking quality, and score reliability. For true positives TP, false positives FP, and false negatives FN, precision is $\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})$, recall is $\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})$, and F1 is their harmonic mean. Precision describes the correctness of predicted ones; recall describes how many labelled ones are recovered. Because ones are rare, these measures accompany the receiver operating characteristic area (ROC-AUC), which summarizes discrimination across thresholds [@saito2015].

Average precision (AP) summarizes the precision-recall trade-off as $\mathrm{AP}=\sum_k(R_k-R_{k-1})P_k$, where $P_k$ and $R_k$ are precision and recall at successive distinct score thresholds. Equal scores are evaluated together. This stepwise definition differs from the trapezoidal area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC); both quantities are retained separately. The implementation follows the noninterpolated convention described in the scikit-learn metric documentation [@sklearnap].

The Brier score is the mean squared difference between score $q_j$ and label $y_j$, $N^{-1}\sum_j(q_j-y_j)^2$ [@brier1950]. Lower values indicate smaller prediction error. Expected calibration error (ECE) compares predicted positive scores with observed positive frequencies within ten equal-width bins over $[0,1]$:

$$\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{10}\frac{|S_b|}{N}\left|\overline q_b-\overline y_b\right|.$$

Here, $S_b$ is a score bin; empty bins contribute zero, and score 1 is assigned to the last bin. This binary positive-score diagnostic follows the binned calibration principle discussed by @guo2017, rather than their multiclass top-label confidence definition. Brier and ECE describe score reliability, while BCE describes the training objective. All are reported with their aggregation convention: variable-pooled metrics combine targets across graphs, whereas parent-macro metrics average independently computed parent scores, giving each instance equal weight.

## Reproducibility and data provenance

The [canonical repository](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/cfl-gurobi-gnn) provides the implementation, split manifest, protocols, dependency specifications, and publication instructions. Original benchmark inputs remain available from MILPBench [@milpbench]. The evidence ledger binds training, validation, and optimization tables to their source artifacts using SHA256 hashes. It preserves complete outcomes and historical attempts separately. Manuscript figures are generated from these fixed tables, and publication builds execute no training, prediction, or optimization.

Experiments ran on UJA DGX-DaSCI at the Higher Polytechnic School of Jaén, University of Jaén. The supplied DGX-1 inventory lists eight 32-GB Tesla V100 GPUs, two 20-core x86 CPUs at 2.2 GHz, and 512 GB memory. This inventory is not a runtime hardware probe and does not imply allocation of all eight GPUs to training. Solver workers use one Gurobi thread; actual Slurm allocations and software versions are recorded per run. Storage includes an OS SATA SSD with a 6 Gb/s interface and a four-device SSD RAID-0 array. Interface capacity is distinguished from measured throughput.

Project-owned code and manuscript material use the MIT License; benchmark, solver, and publisher-template rights retain their respective terms. Shareable evidence excludes license credentials, private paths, raw logs, and model checkpoints. The repository contains the current publication tables and their provenance. The planned Zenodo archive and its DOI status are addressed in the final considerations; no unverified deposit is used as a data-availability claim.

# Results

## Prediction and learning dynamics

The predictive-test graphs contain 5,536,400 binary targets, of which 5,265 take value 1, a prevalence of approximately 0.0951%. @fig-loss shows how training and validation weighted BCE evolve over the 100 epochs and identifies the checkpoint selected by validation.

![Training and validation loss over 100 epochs.](figures/figure_training_validation_loss.pdf){#fig-loss width=95%}

Source: fixed 100-epoch training and validation history.

The solid curve represents training loss and the dashed curve validation loss; the vertical marker identifies epoch 34. Training BCE falls from 1.5877 to 0.0275. Validation BCE reaches a minimum of 0.0510 at the selected epoch and is 0.1124 at epoch 100. The minimum-validation rule therefore selects an earlier checkpoint rather than the final network state. @tbl-predictive reports performance of this selected checkpoint on the held-out predictive graphs.

{{< include tables/current_predictive.qmd >}}

Pooled precision and recall are 0.6923 and 0.7064, respectively, giving F1 of 0.6993. AP is 0.7745, and the separately calculated trapezoidal PR-AUC is 0.7747. The parent-macro F1 of 0.7027 gives a similar picture when each instance receives equal weight. ROC-AUC is 0.99969. The table also records Brier and ECE, enabling score error and calibration to be examined alongside classification performance. These measurements describe prediction; the following subsections assess its effect on optimization.

## Guidance validation

The six-instance validation comparison satisfies the precommitted qualification rule: all learned starts are accepted without abstention, four reduce terminal gap, the median difference is -1.224 percentage points, and one increase exceeds one percentage point. Medium 19 reaches zero terminal gap after approximately 671 seconds, while its unguided control reaches the time limit. The validation observations are displayed alongside the distinct test observations in @fig-effects below; only the validation observations qualify the policy.

## Frozen optimization test

@tbl-heldout compares terminal gaps and first observed 10% crossings for all six optimization-test instances. Each row pairs the unguided and learned-start runs of the same mathematical model. A negative gap difference favors the learned start; a censored crossing indicates that the 10% target was not observed within the budget.

{{< include tables/current_heldout.qmd >}}

Learned starts reduce terminal gap on five of six test instances, with a median paired difference of -1.164 percentage points. The largest decreases occur on medium 20 and 12, whose learned runs finish before the time limit. Medium 0 has a slightly larger terminal gap with guidance despite reaching 10% earlier; medium 4 has a slightly smaller terminal gap but crosses 10% later. Thus, terminal optimality gap and progress during the run provide complementary views. @fig-effects displays the signed gap differences, keeping validation and optimization-test observations in separate panels.

![Paired terminal-gap differences by instance.](figures/figure_validation_test_gap_effects.pdf){#fig-effects width=95%}

Source: fixed validation and optimization-test paired effects.

Each bar compares the learned and unguided run for one medium instance. Bars left of zero indicate a smaller terminal gap with the GNN start; bars right of zero indicate a larger gap. Numeric labels give the difference in percentage points. Panel scales differ to keep smaller effects readable. The validation panel shows four improvements; the test panel shows five, with the pronounced medium-20 effect visible rather than absorbed into an average. @fig-target-time then examines the first observed time to the 10% target for each of the three methods.

![First observed time to a 10% relative gap.](figures/figure_time_to_ten_percent_gap.pdf){#fig-target-time width=95%}

Source: fixed optimization-test worker outcomes.

Shorter observed bars indicate earlier attainment of the target. Hatched bars mark censored observations at the 3,600-second budget boundary, indicated by dotted lines, rather than measured attainment times. The GNN run crosses 10% on four instances, compared with three for each comparator. On medium 20, the learned run crosses while both comparators remain above the target; on medium 12 and 20, its observed crossing times are approximately 672 and 1,168 seconds. All times in this figure concern optimization, with preparation and inference accounted for separately.

## Influence and computational cost

To assess how individual instances affect the aggregate result, @tbl-influence reports the complete six-instance summary and two leave-out diagnostics. The diagnostics retain the original fixed policy and do not redefine the test population.

{{< include tables/current_influence.qmd >}}

The mean paired difference is -7.200 percentage points across all six instances. It is -1.659 points without medium 20 and -0.556 points without medium 12 and 20; the corresponding medians are -1.164, -0.213, and -0.140 points. The favorable direction persists in these diagnostics, while the magnitude changes appreciably. The matched root-LP comparator improves terminal gap on one of six test instances, with a median difference of approximately +1.124 points relative to control. @tbl-times complements the gap results with optimization and worker elapsed times.

{{< include tables/current_timing.qmd >}}

The learned runs on medium 12 and 20 use approximately 702 and 1,585 seconds of optimization. Four learned runs and all six runs of each comparator reach the optimization budget and are right-censored for time to optimality. GNN worker totals exceed optimization times because the worker also verifies artifacts, builds the model, and audits the solution. The table's worker-total column excludes feature preparation and inference, as specified in its note; it describes a different timing scope from a complete cold application.

# Discussion

The results connect assignment prediction with a measurable solver intervention. The network recovers about 71% of labelled positives at roughly 69% precision, and the resulting class-aware starts yield smaller terminal gaps on five of six optimization-test instances. Together, these observations address the research question at both levels: the learned values carry predictive information, and supplying selected values can improve fixed-budget optimization in the examined setting.

This connection follows the L2O perspective of @bengio2021: learning is valuable when it improves a decision within an optimization procedure. Like the starting-scenario approach of @goerigk2025, our method learns information that initializes a conventional solution algorithm. The objects differ, however: their classifier selects scenarios, whereas ours selects variable values. In contrast to the constraint-generating integration of @qu2026, our partial start preserves the original feasible region. This distinction is important when interpreting the solver's subsequent objective bounds.

The bipartite representation makes the proposal consistent with the structural learning approach of @gasse2019, but changes the target from branching to primal assignments. The favorable test-gap pattern complements the prediction-guided primal methods of @ding2020, @khalil2022, and @canturk2024. It also supports the practical rationale behind optimizer-completed partial assignments in @nair2020: a useful suggestion need not specify an entire solution. The class-aware construction gives this principle a concrete form for sparse binary positives, retaining predicted ones before filling the remaining support with zeros.

The root-LP comparison provides an additional perspective. Because the two starts contain equally many values and equally many ones, their different outcomes concern which variables receive those values. The GNN improves gap on five test instances, compared with one for the matched relaxation-based start. This pattern is consistent with useful learned ordering information rather than a benefit from supplying an arbitrary start of the same size. It motivates further examination of the interaction between graph-derived scores and partial-start completion, rather than attributing the effect to network accuracy alone.

Prediction quality and optimization progress also need different interpretations. Precision and recall focus attention on rare positive targets, as advocated for imbalanced classification by @saito2015. Brier and ECE complement that view by describing score error and reliability [@brier1950; @guo2017]. The terminal gap reflects both the feasible objective and the dual bound: a smaller gap does not necessarily mean a smaller feasible objective in every pair. Gap and time to the 10% target also capture different aspects of progress, as medium 0 and 4 illustrate. The separate predictive and optimization assessments therefore clarify how learned information is used by the solver.

# Final considerations, limitations and future work

This study set out to determine whether a bipartite GNN could provide useful starting values for medium CFL optimization. The implemented offline-to-online procedure meets that objective in the examined development setting: it learns from checked original-instance solutions, constructs class-aware partial starts, and produces favorable terminal-gap differences on five of six test instances without changing the mathematical model. The median improvement is 1.164 percentage points, and two learned runs complete before the optimization limit. These findings establish a practical demonstration and a reproducible basis for further investigation.

Several limitations define its scope. The experiment uses one seed and six optimization-test instances; the influence analysis shows that two instances account for much of the mean effect. The observations do not establish population-level statistical significance or a general speedup. Four learned runs and all comparator runs remain censored for time to optimality. Detailed preparation and inference costs are retained upstream but are not included in the transferred publication timing table, so cold end-to-end acceleration cannot be quantified from that table alone. The root-LP comparator depends on the learned start's support and positive count, and an independent random-support comparison has not been completed.

Solution labels are feasible but may be approximate, and the 10% admission ceiling selects instances that the solver can already solve to that quality. Alternative good solutions can differ from the supervised label. Consequently, score agreement and calibration are not equivalent to solution quality. The earlier easy-only engineering pilot had mixed outcomes: guided gap improved from 6.753% to 6.391% on medium 0 but worsened from 7.172% to 7.830% on medium 1, and guided elapsed cost increased. Validation of the revised policy also includes increases of 2.326 and 0.735 percentage points on medium 11 and 17. These cases remain in the evidence and preclude attributing the improvement solely to the selector, since the training population also changed.

The full 90-instance experiment, a hard-instance demonstration, and a controlled augmentation comparison have not been completed. Longer exploratory hard solves did not meet the label-admission ceiling; this is a computational outcome, not evidence of mathematical infeasibility. Current training uses Gurobi-labelled original instances, so the reported gains are not attributed to synthetic augmentation.

Future experiments should replicate the comparison with additional independently frozen seeds and instances, quantify parent-level uncertainty, and isolate the effects of class-aware ordering, support size, calibration, and training population. Independent root-LP and random-support baselines would strengthen interpretation. Extension to the remaining medium and hard instances requires budget and resource studies that retain every outcome and avoid selecting experiments retrospectively by success.

A second direction is controlled augmentation from checked Gurobi and SCIP incumbents. For incumbent $\bar x$, local branching [@fischetti2003] defines a descendant by adding

$$\sum_{j\in B_p:\bar x_j=0}x_j+\sum_{j\in B_p:\bar x_j=1}(1-x_j)\leq k.$$

Each descendant requires its own model, graph, and independently checked label. It must inherit its original parent's partition, remain training-only, and be treated as a correlated sample. Comparisons with original-only training should match parent sampling mass and optimizer-step budgets. Further work can examine bipartite communities and variable/constraint roles through network-science methods, complementing PCA and UMAP visualizations.

Finally, a curated Zenodo dataset is planned for intermediate LP models, bipartite graphs, produced embeddings, and principal results, including unsuccessful attempts. The source ledger already preserves these outcomes; the archive requires a redistribution-rights review and verified deposition. A DOI has not yet been verified as reserved or published. Once the draft and DOI are confirmed, the data-availability statement will identify the versioned record and distinguish reserved identification from public availability.
